frames.narration: A shopper opens product 481. The application server asks its small in-process cache first. It has 5,000 entries and does not have this one.
The key is hashed and placed on the ring. The next shard clockwise is shard 3 of 8, so the router sends the read there. Adding or losing a shard would move only about 1 in 8 of the keys.

Shard 3 has the entry. It moves the entry to the front of its linked list, a handful of pointer changes whatever the size of the cache, and returns the 2 KB value in about a millisecond. The database is not touched.
The value is stored in the in-process cache, in the probation segment. A second read of product 481 a moment later promotes it to the protected segment, where it stays as long as it keeps being used.

At the same time the nightly report reads 20,000 old products once each. They are sent with a no-store flag, and any that do get in only fill the probation segment. They never reach the protected hot items, so the hit rate for shoppers stays where it was.

At the peak of a sale the entry for a popular product expires. 1,500 reads a second ask for it. The first one is let through to the database; the other 74 or so that arrive during the 50 ms query wait for its answer. Meanwhile the old value is served as stale for up to a few seconds.
The refill finishes and every waiting request gets the same value. The new entry gets a TTL with random jitter added, so entries stored together do not all expire together next time.

A merchandiser changes the price of product 481. The change is published as an event, and the event removes the entry from shard 3 and from every in-process cache. The next read fetches the new price, and the TTL stays only as the backstop in case an event is lost.
